title: Token Costs Are Becoming The New EDA Budget Battle
gist: A roundtable of EDA and agentic-AI executives (from Cadence, Keysight, Siemens EDA, Synopsys, and ChipAgents) reveals that token costs for agentic AI in chip design have gone from a non-issue a year ago to a ballooning, uncapped line item now rivaling mask-cost economics, pushing the industry toward open-source/fine-tuned models, model routers, and token-budget controls even as engineers insist expensive physics-based verification can never be skipped because a single bad tapeout can bankrupt a chip company.

themes.theme: Token costs have become an uncontrolled, structural budget line

insights.claim: According to Cadence's Matt Graham, design, verification, and implementation teams only started asking seriously about token efficiency, token budgets, and how to budget for agentic AI tool deployment in the last three to four weeks before this discussion, whereas a year earlier nobody cared about token costs.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The sudden (weeks-old) shift to token-cost scrutiny signals EDA vendors' near-term deal conversations and pricing models are being actively renegotiated right now — a live inflection point for EDA vendor revenue models.
insights.quote: Last year, nobody cared.

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr argued that EDA/design budgets used to be fixed and predictable (customers negotiated a cost per engineer and per chip to project total budget), but token budgets are not fixed and are now ballooning out of proportion, making it hard for chipmakers to estimate final chip price even as agentic AI lets them design more chips (e.g., 10 instead of 2) with the same engineering headcount.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A structural shift from fixed EDA cost structures to variable, compute-consumption-based token costs changes how chip companies model project economics and could compress margins on chip programs that don't tightly control token spend.
insights.quote: EDA budgets used to be fixed. They're not fixed anymore. That creates the issue of how to estimate the chip price when you have a ballooning budget at the bottom that you can't control.
insights.locator: Petr quote on fixed vs ballooning budgets

insights.claim: Petr predicted that next year the industry discussion will shift decisively to token efficiency as the main issue, with customers moving toward small language models (SLMs) and limiting token expense in order to make costs predictable, because currently 'every CFO just opens up their wallet because they don't know what else to do.'
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A named, dated prediction (token efficiency becomes THE issue 'next year') gives investors a concrete timeline to watch for EDA vendor commentary shifting toward cost-control features and SLM partnerships.
insights.quote: My prediction is that next year, that discussion will be completely different. We will see token efficiency as the main issue. We will see customers trying to go with SLMs (small language models)

insights.claim: Synopsys' Anand Thiruvengadam confirmed the shift is already happening: discussions with many customers have moved from unlimited token/dollar budgets to restricting tokens or dollars at the individual engineering level, which is also driving a trend toward open-source models.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Per-engineer token/dollar caps are a concrete, implementable cost-control mechanism now in production use at Synopsys customers — a leading indicator for how enterprise AI tool consumption gets metered and budgeted across the industry.
insights.quote: It's already becoming a reality. With many of our customers, the discussions have shifted from unlimited budgets to restricting, at the engineering level, a certain number of tokens or dollars.

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Harrison Balistreri projected tokens-per-engineer-per-year will reach 100 billion within the next 18 months based on current usage trends, and described the token budgeting/ROI conversation as already a present-day reality for customers, not something arriving next year.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A concrete forward number (100 billion tokens per engineer per year within 18 months) gives a quantifiable growth trajectory for AI-driven compute/token demand specifically originating from chip design workflows — a data point for modeling AI infrastructure and inference-cost demand from the EDA sector specifically.
insights.quote: We see tokens per engineer per year going to 100 billion in the next 18 months, based on trends in how people use our products.

insights.claim: Petr noted that some companies have run the math and concluded that a human engineer is cheaper than running an agent for the same job, implying agentic AI ROI is not universally positive today.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A direct counter to the industry narrative that agentic AI is unambiguously cost-saving — investors should discount vendor ROI claims for agentic AI tools until token-efficiency and fine-tuning work matures further.
insights.quote: A fun fact here is that some companies do the math and say, 'Hey, an engineer is cheaper than having an agent running for the same job.'
insights.locator: Petr quote on engineer vs agent cost

themes.theme: Physical verification is the hard floor AI cannot skip

insights.claim: Keysight's Petr argued there is 'no such thing as trust' in chip design when a TSMC mask set costs multi-million to hundreds of millions of dollars — only 'trust and verify' — because physical multiphysics simulation (thermal, power) is the final arbiter regardless of how much digital/analog design or agentic reasoning preceded it; getting the thermal or power budget wrong means the IC burns.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: This sets a hard ceiling on how far agentic AI can compress chip design cost/time — physical verification via multiphysics engines remains a non-negotiable, expensive gate that no amount of LLM reasoning can bypass, limiting the addressable cost savings from agentic AI in EDA.
insights.quote: If a TSMC mask set costs you multi-million dollars, or hundreds of million dollars, there is no such thing as trust. There's only trust and verify... If you got the power wrong, it's going to burn.
insights.locator: Petr's extended answer on trust and verify

insights.claim: Petr drew a direct analogy to software engineering's 'AI slop' problem — where nobody understands code an agent generated until a service like AWS goes down from an update — warning that letting agent swarms design chips humans wouldn't design (exploiting parasitic effects as a 'feature') risks an equivalent failure mode in silicon, where a bad tapeout ('mask head is wrong') can bankrupt the company outright ('most likely goes belly up'), unlike software which can be patched.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: This is a sharp, quotable risk framing: unlike software AI slop (fixable via patch), chip AI slop is existential and irreversible once taped out — a key risk factor for any company aggressively adopting agentic AI in physical chip design, especially for large AI chips where a single mistake is catastrophic.
insights.quote: You get this wrong the first time, you're dead in the water. Your company most likely goes belly up.
insights.locator: Petr on AI slop analogy and mask failure

insights.claim: Cadence's Graham argued the AI-accelerated chip design process 'doesn't remove the requirements' of proven design methodology — AI can accelerate output, but the next inflection point is that wasted or not, token budget is becoming a large enough fraction of mask costs that it now matters materially to project economics, unlike a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Frames token cost as now comparable in materiality to mask cost — a threshold crossing worth tracking in EDA vendor and chip-design-house cost disclosures going forward.
insights.quote: The point is that the token budget, wasted or not, is becoming a big enough percentage of those mask costs that it's starting to matter.

themes.theme: Open-source and fine-tuned models are winning on cost predictability

insights.claim: Petr argued that if a company wants predictable CapEx it can depreciate over years, it should 'put a frontier model on it' — implying open-source/self-hosted models are increasingly chosen specifically for cost predictability (treated like depreciable infrastructure) rather than for capability, and that discussion of exactly which model underlies a workflow is often deliberately obscured.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Treating an AI model choice as a CapEx depreciation decision rather than a pure capability decision is a notable shift in how enterprises are financially structuring AI tool spend — relevant to how EDA and chip-design customers will procure AI going forward.
insights.quote: If you want CapEx that is predictable, which you can depreciate over a certain number of years, put a frontier model on it. The whole discussion of where it comes from is kind of under the table.

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Sathish Balasubramanian said customers are getting smarter about model selection, reserving frontier/latest models only for the hardest roughly 2% of design-flow tasks and using open-source models for the initial design phase or tasks that don't need frontier capability, because open-source models can handle 98% of the work; he compared using a frontier model for routine work to 'using a Ferrari for their daily grocery run.'
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The 98%/2% task-complexity split is a concrete, reusable segmentation for evaluating where frontier-model spend is actually justified in enterprise AI deployment — relevant well beyond chip design, to any enterprise AI cost-optimization strategy.
insights.quote: Six months ago, everyone was using a Ferrari for their daily grocery run. That doesn't make sense at all... It is just the 2% very extreme [part of the design flow] that needs the greatest models.

insights.claim: Balasubramanian said Siemens EDA demonstrated LLM routing for long-running agents with Nvidia, and separately cited Switchboard (an AI-powered communication platform) and Nvidia as having 'a very good way of routing LLMs' to match specific workflows to specific models — open-source appeal is amplified because customers can then air-gap systems, run on-prem, and encrypt data.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Model routing plus on-prem/air-gapped open-source deployment is becoming the concrete technical architecture for cost-and-security-conscious enterprise AI adoption in chip design — a pattern EDA vendors are actively building and could productize as a differentiator.
insights.quote: What we are seeing is that customers are getting much smarter. They are not giving out the latest and greatest models... for the initial phase of design, or designs that don't really need them.
insights.locator: Balasubramanian quote on customer model choices

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Balistreri said its bespoke agent loops run 40-50% cheaper than baseline on the same tasks using the same underlying Opus model, and that ChipAgents released its own host-trained, open-weight model that performs similarly to frontier models on chip-specific, long-horizon SoC-level tasks but at 5X lower cost, driven by customer demand for secure on-premises deployment.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A specific, named vendor claim (5X cost reduction via a comparably performant open-weight model) is a concrete competitive benchmark for evaluating agentic-AI EDA vendors' cost claims against each other.
insights.quote: If you look at what we've done in our bespoke loops, side by side with the same baseline, we are 40% to 50% cheaper on the same tasks... We released our own host-trained, open-weight model that performs similarly to frontier models on chip-specific tasks with long horizons and difficult SoC-level tasks, but it's 5X cheaper.
insights.locator: Balistreri quote on bespoke loops and open-weight model

insights.claim: Balistreri cited a specific example where Moonshot AI's Kimi model (K3 AI) delivered a full chip design for $48 in token cost, but noted the outcome quality is comparable to 'making a car that can only go one mile an hour' — implying cheap-but-inadequate results — and argued true full-flow autonomous ROI requires ontology, flow capture, and harness optimization layered on top of any underlying model, not just a cheap model alone.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The $48-chip anecdote is a vivid, quotable data point illustrating that raw token-cost minimization without workflow enablement produces unusable results — a caution against judging agentic AI vendors purely on cost-per-token metrics.
insights.quote: Right now, the Kimi model (K3 AI by Chinese startup Moonshot AI) delivered a chip at $48. I heard someone say that's like making a car that can only go one mile an hour.
insights.locator: Balistreri quote on Kimi chip cost

insights.claim: Petr argued that 'open models are six months behind frontier models,' but that '[s]ix months is infinity right now' given the pace of AI progress, meaning he would readily take an open-source model from six months in the future today because it would already be a decade ahead of where open models are now — implying rapid convergence between open and frontier model capability over time, after which competitive differentiation shifts entirely to the enablement/workflow layer.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: If open-source/frontier model capability gaps continue closing this fast, EDA and agentic-AI vendors' durable moat shifts decisively away from which underlying LLM they use and toward proprietary workflow/enablement/context-capture IP — a key thesis for how to value competing EDA-AI vendors long term.
insights.quote: Open models are six months behind frontier models. Six months is infinity right now. If you ask me today, 'Do I want the open-source model from [six months in the future], I would say, 'Hell yeah,' because I know it's going to be a decade further in the future.

themes.theme: The real moat is workflow/context capture, not the model itself

insights.claim: Petr argued that the underlying LLM 'is the least important thing in the whole stack nowadays' and that the real work and value lie in flow capturing — extracting an organization's implicit, unspoken engineering knowledge and encoding it into deterministic skills and tools that sit on top of any chosen model, meaning more time invested in workflow enablement makes any LLM (even a cheaper one like Kimi) more capable.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: This is a direct investment thesis implication: value in agentic-AI-for-EDA accrues to whoever captures proprietary organizational workflow/context (a defensible, hard-to-replicate asset), not to whoever licenses the best foundation model — a key differentiator for evaluating EDA AI vendors like Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, and ChipAgents.
insights.quote: The LLM itself is the least important thing in the whole stack nowadays. Everything else, including the enablement... that is where the real work lies.

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Balistreri distinguished 'local context' (available to most generic agent/LLM schemes) from 'global context' — the unsaid, unspoken knowledge between teams and individuals — arguing ChipAgents does substantial work mapping this global context into flows across organizations to deliver ROI, operating at the agent-loop/harness level, the organizational-flow level, and the model level simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The local-vs-global-context framework is a reusable mental model for evaluating any enterprise agentic-AI vendor's true differentiation — vendors that only wrap a generic LLM without capturing global/tacit organizational context are more easily commoditized.
insights.quote: There's local context that most agents can use in generic LLM schemes, but what you need is the global context. You need what is unsaid and unspoken between teams and individuals.
insights.locator: Balistreri quote on local vs global context

insights.claim: Balistreri argued the moat is not just enablement/workflow capture but also fine-tuning the model itself on a customer's own data, libraries, and chip designs, since base-model performance — even for large open-source models — 'just isn't there yet' for full-flow autonomous outcomes without post-training.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts Petr's 'LLM is least important' framing — a live disagreement among panelists about whether fine-tuning or pure workflow enablement is the more durable differentiator, worth tracking as vendors' product strategies diverge.
insights.quote: Base-model performance, even for larger open-source models, just isn't there yet... you can't just take a model out of the box and do it if you're trying to compare with the frontier models.

insights.claim: Cadence's Graham noted that if software capability can be subsumed into the model over time, fine-tuning can probably be subsumed even more easily, raising an open question about whether the industry converges on fine-tuned models, a hard/easy-problem usage bifurcation, or some combination, plus how much air-gapping enterprises will require — he stated these questions 'have no clear answers' yet.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: An explicit admission from a senior EDA executive that the industry has not converged on a winning architecture for enterprise agentic AI deployment — signals continued volatility/optionality in vendor strategy and product bets over the next year.
insights.quote: It will be very interesting to see [what wins] in another year. Is it fine-tuned models? Is it a bifurcation of the usage between hard and easy problems?... These are all questions that have no clear answers.

insights.claim: Synopsys' Thiruvengadam identified tool literacy and workflow literacy (an engineer's fluency with tools transferred to the AI system so it calls LLMs more efficiently) plus a deployable model router that assesses task nature and complexity to choose which model to use, as concrete, currently-deployed levers ('We are doing it already') to reduce token cost.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Model routing based on task complexity is presented as an already-shipping Synopsys capability, not a roadmap item — a concrete near-term product differentiator to watch in Synopsys' AI tooling disclosures.
insights.quote: We can deploy a model router that looks at the nature of the task and its complexity, then decides which model to use. Those are the ways you can further reduce the token cost.
